recipe.history:
The cucumber is one of humanity's oldest cultivated vegetables, with origins stretching back more than three thousand years to the Indian subcontinent. Ancient Sanskrit texts reference the plant, and archaeological evidence places cucumber cultivation in western Asia as far back as 9000 BCE. From India it traveled westward along trade routes into the Middle East and the Mediterranean, where Greek and Roman civilizations embraced it with enthusiasm. The Romans reportedly grew cucumbers year-round using a primitive greenhouse system, and Emperor Tiberius was said to demand cucumbers on his table every single day. In France, where Brie cheese also finds its roots, the cucumber became a staple of refined cuisine, prized for its cooling, clean flavor that balanced richer ingredients on the plate.

Cucumber made its way into American kitchens through European settlers who brought seeds from England, Germany, and France. By the nineteenth century it was a fixture in home gardens across the eastern seaboard. In American cuisine, the cucumber's crisp, hydrating quality made it a natural counterpoint to the heat and fat of grilled meats. Ribbon salads — thin, translucent shavings of cucumber dressed in light vinegar — became a beloved Southern summer preparation. The pairing of cucumber with soft, creamy cheeses like Brie followed naturally, as the cool crunch of the vegetable cut through the lush, buttery paste of the cheese. When burger culture exploded in post-war America, inventive cooks began layering these contrasting textures onto patties, discovering that the combination created something far more complex than the sum of its parts.

I remember the first time I made a cucumber ribbon salad for a burger. It was a sweltering July afternoon, the kind where the air sits on you like a wet blanket, and I had a block of Brie left over from a dinner party sitting in the fridge. I shaved the cucumber into long, pale green ribbons with a vegetable peeler, tossed them in a little rice wine vinegar and a pinch of salt, and let them wilt slightly while the Brie sliced and softened at room temperature. When I draped those ribbons over a still-sizzling patty and laid the Brie on top to melt under the broiler, the kitchen smelled like summer and France at the same time. My daughter wandered in, took one look, and said it was the prettiest burger she had ever seen. She wasn't wrong.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at the center — is not a preference. It is a commitment to the truth of beef. At this temperature, the myoglobin in the meat remains rosy and alive, the fat has begun to render and coat every fiber with flavor, and the texture is yielding without being slack. Going beyond this point is a slow erasure: at medium, nuance begins to fade; at well done, you are eating something that was once a burger. The Maillard crust on the outside provides all the caramelized, savory complexity you need, while the interior stays juicy, pink, and honest. Brie melts beautifully at this serving temperature, flowing into the crust and the cucumber ribbons without becoming greasy. Medium rare is not a risk — it is a respect paid to the animal, the farmer, and every person who will sit down to eat.
ingredients: 6 tbsp unsalted butter, softened and cubed
8 oz Brie cheese, rind trimmed, sliced 1/4-inch thick
Salt and white pepper to taste
instructions: 1. Make the brioche buns: Dissolve yeast in warm milk with 1 tsp sugar; let bloom 10 minutes until foamy.
2. In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine flour, remaining sugar, and salt. Add the yeast mixture and eggs; mix on low until a shaggy dough forms, about 3 minutes.

3. Increase speed to medium; add butter one cube at a time, waiting for each piece to incorporate before adding the next. This will take 8–10 minutes. The dough should be smooth, glossy, and pull away cleanly from the bowl.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8–12 hours) for a slow, cold rise.

5. Divide chilled dough into 4 equal portions (about 120g each). Shape into tight rounds by pulling the dough underneath itself and pinching. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and proof at room temperature 2–3 hours until doubled and puffy.
6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns gently with egg wash; sprinkle sesame seeds if using. Bake 18–20 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack at least 30 minutes before slicing.

7. Make the cucumber ribbon salad: Using a vegetable peeler, shave the cucumber into long, thin ribbons, rotating the cucumber as you go and stopping when you reach the seedy core. Place ribbons in a colander, toss with salt, and let sit 10 minutes to draw out moisture.

8. Gently squeeze the cucumber ribbons to remove excess liquid. In a bowl, whisk together rice wine vinegar, sugar, dill, mint, and white pepper. Add cucumbers and toss to coat. Refrigerate until ready to serve.
9. Make the herb mayo: Whisk together mayonnaise, chives, lemon juice, and Dijon. Season with salt and white pepper. Cover and refrigerate.

10. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 6 oz each). Gently form into patties roughly 3/4-inch thick and slightly wider than the buns (they will shrink during cooking). Press a shallow dimple in the center of each with your thumb. Season generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder on both sides.
11. Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Add butter and swirl to coat.
12. Place patties in the skillet without crowding. Cook undisturbed 3–4 minutes until a deep mahogany crust forms. Flip once.

13. Immediately lay Brie slices over each patty, covering the surface. Cook an additional 2–3 minutes. To encourage the Brie to melt fully, tent loosely with a sheet of foil for the final 90 seconds. Pull patties when an instant-read thermometer inserted in the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes on a wire rack.
14. While patties rest, split the brioche buns and toast cut-side down in the residual fat in the skillet for 60–90 seconds until golden.
15. Assemble the burgers: Spread herb mayo generously on both cut surfaces of each bun. Place a butter lettuce leaf on the bottom bun, followed by a tomato slice seasoned with flaky sea salt.
16. Set the Brie-crowned patty on top of the tomato. Lift the cucumber ribbons from the dressing with tongs, letting excess liquid drip off, and drape a generous nest of ribbons over the melted Brie.
17. Close with the top bun, pressing gently so the Brie and cucumbers settle. Serve immediately.
